title: "Policy"
---

This section will look at New York City, USA as a case study city, with their the [OneNYC 2050](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/climate/downloads/pdfs/OneNYC_2050_Strategic_Plan.pdf) strategy's goal to achieve "A Liveable Climate". Like most dense urban areas, New York City (NYC) is also facing the problems of warmer urban temperatures than its rural and suburban neighborhoods. Given growing events of higher frequency, longer lasting and more intense heat waves, this section will focus on one of NYC's experiencing climate threats of [Extreme Heat](https://www.nyc.gov/content/climate/pages/extreme-heat).

## Summary

The OneNYC 2050: Building a Strong and Fair City is a long term strategic plan compromised of 8 goals and 30 initiatives. It aims to achieve an equitable, sustainable and thriving city through addressing its climate change, economic equality, housing, health, education, transportation and infrastructure. Under its "Livable Climate" goal, the strategy sets out the following key initiatives in repsonse to NYC's climate threats. Initiative 21 is directly relevant to the extreme heat challenge, envisioning community level interventions that aims to reduce vulnerability to climate impacts such as rising temperatures.

+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| A Livable Climate Initiatives, OneNYC 2050 Strategic Plan                                                        |
+==================================================================================================================+
| 20. Achieve carbon neutrality and 100 percent clean electricity                                                  |
| 21. A LIVABLE CLIMATE Strengthen communities, buildings, infrastructure, and the waterfront to be more resilient |
| 22. Create economic opportunities for all New Yorkers through climate action                                     |
| 23. Fight for climate accountability and justice                                                                 |
+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

: Relevant Initiatives, Source: [OneNYC 2050](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/climate/downloads/pdfs/OneNYC_2050_Strategic_Plan.pdf)

NYC has identified extreme heat to be one of its major climate threats, where it "is now the number one cause of mortality from weather conditions" ([OneNYC 2050](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/climate/downloads/pdfs/OneNYC_2050_Strategic_Plan.pdf), p.32). Extreme heat within the city also known as the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect, is a challenge that is widely faced by many cities globally. These neighbourhoods tends to have concentrations dark surfaces from built structures, concrete and asphalt that absorbs and retain solar radiation throughout the day, while having limited green space to facilitate natural cooling through evapotranspiration and solar shading. The NYC has also identified limited access to air conditioning, energy costs and poor housing quality as drivers of such heat impacts ([Nyc.gov, 2019](https://www.nyc.gov/content/climate/pages/extreme-heat)).

::: {layout-ncol="1"}
![UHI, Source: [EARTH.ORG](https://earth.org/data_visualization/urban-heat-islands/)](images/w4_images/UHIfig1.jpg)
:::

"All heat deaths are preventable" ([Nyc.gov, 2019](https://www.nyc.gov/content/climate/pages/extreme-heat)). The OneNYC uses the Heat Vulnerability Index to identify neighborhoods that are more at risk following extreme heat. The risks are not evenly distributed across the city, where South Bronx, Central Brooklyn and Upper Manhattan are highlighted as the city's most heat vulnerable neighborhoods.

::: {layout-ncol="1"}
![HVI (Data Source: [EJNYC Full Data Explorer](https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/6a3da7b920f248af961554bdf01d668b) )](images/w4_images/NYC_HVI_Map2.png)
:::

In action, the OneNYC strategy supports scientific based decision-making, and is commited to ensure that policies and physical actions are protective and cost effective. It is commited to intervene through a range of nature-based and built solutions, such as promoting urban forests efforts to combat extreme heat, installation of cool roofs to lower local temperatures and mitigate the health impacts from UHI as well as further green infrastructure investments. Next will be looked at how remotely sensed data could be used to address policy goals.

## Application

### Data

Land surface temperature (LST) obtained from satellite sensors are particularly useful for understanding and mapping extreme heat. The Landsat Thematic Mapper (TM)/Enhanced Thematic Mapper (ETM+)/Thermal Infrared Sensor (TIRS) and Terra/Aqua Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) are commonly used for urban heat studies, accounting for around 78% of total publications ([Zhou et. al., 2019](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/11/1/48)). This reflected how widely remotely sensing satellite data has been adopted for research in this field.

Another approach is the ground based temperature sensors. The observations allow monitoring and studying of the urban boundary layer, which is the layer above the city where heat and moisture exchanges. It has been identified for ability to provide monitoring and long term conditions of locations, which complements remotely sensing data for NYC ([Solecki et.al., 2015](https://nyaspubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1111/nyas.12587)).

### Limitations and Integrated Approaches

Despite the value of satellite data of addressing extreme heat, there are still several limitations in measuring urban heat. [Shandas et.al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2225-1154/7/1/5)(2019) discussed two commonly used approaches of ground based temperature and satellite imagery to estimate surface temperatures. Thermal infrared sensors from satellite data record the hotness of physical surfaces, but this will not be the same case of what air temperature humans experiences at street level. For a city where extreme heat can cause deaths, this approach alone may not be enough.

Integrating both methods can enable higher accuracy and precision ([Mushore et.al., 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/15/23/5461) ; [Solecki et.al., 2015](https://nyaspubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1111/nyas.12587)). Further installing high-resolution thermal comfort measuring instruments that are fairly distributed across the city, can and enhance remotely sensing data's utility ([Mushore et.al., 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/15/23/5461) ; [Solecki et.al., 2015](https://nyaspubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1111/nyas.12587)). This is especially beneficial for NYC since heat vulnerability were concentrated in specific neighborhoods, such ground based instruments can improve heat monitoring, providing timely and realistic approaches to respond to heat risks.

## Reflection

This section deepened my understanding of policy and remotely sensing data's role in addressing urban climate challenges. Remotely sensing data provides spatial evidence that bridges between policy objectives and decision-makings. This allowed translation of visionary strategies into actionable solutions.

Municipality policies and goals tends to be a overall vision of actions, governance and goals. The OneBYC although did not detail in remotely sensing methods, but NYC works often involve tools that derives data from remotely sensing systems.

Many studies relied on satellite-based thermal infrared (TIR) data. A key insight is that it could be a limitation, as it captures purely surface temperature but not the temperature that humans experience at street level. This matters in dense neighborhoods where the urban form shapes heat exposure and health risk. This enables observations of variation of temperature across different land uses and land covers, providing a more throughout assessment of urban heat across the city. Critically, this method is more expensive and resource intensive for a large installation coverage.

This section also reinforced that data and visionary policies alone does not bring resilience. [Mushore et.al. (2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/15/23/5461)) have suggested the need of urban greening strategies to be scaled up to municipal level to be economically viable and effective. Without sustained investment and coordination across all boroughs as well as political support, OneNYC 2050's initiatives may remain a short fall otherwise.

On a global context, OneNYC showed its commitments in supporting global initiatives The UN Beat the Heat Handbook identifies urban greening, cool surfaces and planning practices as essential components of city-level heat resilience, closely mirroring OneNYC's approach ([UNEP, 2021](https://www.unep.org/resources/report/beating-heat-sustainable-cooling-handbook-cities)) . The UN SDGs, particularly SDG 3, SDG 11 and SDG 13. This reinforced that OneNYC's approach is not only a local target, but responding to global initiatives and goals.

Overall, OneNYC 2050 provides a positive, sustainable and ambitious strategy for addressing extreme heat, and the sucessfulness will depend on collaboration across city-level legislation, regulation, and governance structures, alongside the economic resources and technical capacity for collecting, processing and interpreting remotely sensed data. Without all rounded collaborations, remotely sensing data will not be utilised to its optimum potential for translation to actionable solutions. Remotely sensing data remains significant potential in monitoring and understanding urban heat, critical for informing policy decision-makings.
